match.reason: The bank point covers Pythagoras' theorem more broadly, including finding the hypotenuse and a 3D box diagonal, and its questions test those rather than finding a shorter side, so it does not match this narrower point.

draft.title: Pythagoras' theorem: shorter side
card: In a right-angled triangle, c² = a² + b², where c is the hypotenuse. The hypotenuse is always the longest side.
To find a shorter side, rearrange to a² = c² − b². Square the hypotenuse, subtract the square of the known short side, then take the square root.
Take care to subtract, not add. A shorter side must come out smaller than the hypotenuse.
Example: the hypotenuse is 10 and one short side is 6. a² = 10² − 6² = 100 − 36 = 64. So a = √64 = 8.
draft.remember: Hypotenuse squared, minus the known short side squared, then the square root.

a.q: A right-angled triangle has a hypotenuse of 17 cm and one short side of 8 cm. What is the other short side?
a.why: a² = 17² − 8² = 289 − 64 = 225, and √225 = 15. Choosing 9 subtracts the sides without squaring them. Choosing 225 forgets the square root.
a.clue: Subtract the squares, then take the root.

b.q: A 13 m ladder leans against a vertical wall. Its foot is 5 m from the wall on level ground. How high up the wall does the ladder reach?
b.why: The ladder is the hypotenuse: a² = 13² − 5² = 169 − 25 = 144, and √144 = 12. Choosing 14 adds the squares, which would give a length longer than the ladder. Choosing 8 subtracts without squaring.
b.clue: The ladder is the longest side, so it goes first.

problems.detail: Why (b) says choosing 14 'adds the squares', but √(13² + 5²) = √194 ≈ 13.9, not exactly 14. A student who checks the working may be confused. It would be clearer to say it is about 14.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer (15 cm and 12 m), and the card and its worked example are correct. One small issue: why (b) treats 14 as the exact result of adding the squares, when √194 is about 13.9.
